Fair point. That was muddy. Let’s clean it up. 🛠️

What “EAS” means

EAS = Expo Application Services

It’s Expo’s cloud build system.
Instead of building the Android app entirely on your own machine, you run a command and Expo builds it for you online.

So when I said:

“Or if you’re using EAS”

I meant:

“If your project is using Expo’s cloud build service instead of only local builds on your computer.”

In plain English

You usually have two ways to get an Android build:

1. Local build

Built on your computer

Examples:

Bash
npx expo run:android

This is usually for local testing on a connected device/emulator.

2. EAS build

Built in Expo’s cloud

Examples:

Bash
npx eas build --platform android --profile preview

This is usually for installable app files, testing builds, and store submission builds.

Based on our past work

You’ve almost certainly been using EAS already when you did commands like:

  • eas build

  • preview builds

  • Android install/test builds from Expo’s system

So you do not need to guess. If Cody or the terminal has had you run eas build, then yes, you’ve been using EAS.

The easiest way to tell

In your project folder, if you’ve run commands like:

Bash
npx eas build --platform android --profile preview

then you are using EAS.

If you’ve only been doing stuff like:

Bash
npx expo start
npx expo run:android

then that’s local/dev workflow.

What I should have said instead

For you, the safer wording would have been:

If you want an installable Android test build:

Bash
npx eas build --platform android --profile preview

That’s the one most likely relevant to your current workflow.

What to do right now

If your goal is:

“I want a real Android build I can install and test”

use:

Bash

If your goal is:

“I just want to run it locally right now from my computer”

use:

npx expo run:android

Best guess for your situation

because that gives you the kind of build you can actually install and test more like a real app.

ChatGPT said:

Got it. Then here is the straight answer:

Your build command

The command you normally run is the right testing build command:

Bash
eas build -p android --profile preview

That creates a preview build through Expo’s cloud build service, which is good for testing on phones before store release. Expo’s docs describe EAS Build as the way to create preview builds and ready-to-submit binaries. Expo Documentation+2Expo Documentation+2

What “finished” actually means for your app

For your goal, there are really two finish lines:

1. Testable build

You already have that workflow:

Bash
eas build -p android --profile preview

2. Store-ready release

After the app is stable enough, you move to a production/release build and submit that to Google Play. EAS supports building the binary that is meant for store submission. Expo Documentation+1

The important reality about invites and installs

This part matters most:

An invite cannot normally “just add the app to their phone”

On Android, the normal install flow is still through Google Play. Google’s own help docs describe app install as happening through the Play Store flow, and Google’s Play linking docs are about sending users to your app’s Play page. Google Help+1

So the realistic polished experience is:

  • If PartyPlus is already installed: invite link opens the app directly

  • If PartyPlus is not installed: invite link sends them to the Play Store listing to install it

  • After install: future invite links can open the app directly via Android App Links

That is the standard, correct path on Android. Android App Links are specifically for opening verified website URLs in the app when it is installed. Android Developers+2Android Developers+2

There is a newer Google Play “inline install” feature, but Google describes it as a test feature for integrating install UI without leaving the current app context. That is not the normal expectation for a simple invite webpage flow. Android Developers

So your actual next objective is this

Not “make the invite install the app automatically.”

Your real target is:

Make the invite flow behave like this

  1. Tap invite link

  2. If app installed, open PartyPlus straight to the party

  3. If app not installed, open PartyPlus Play Store page

  4. User installs

  5. From then on, invite links open in PartyPlus

That is professional, realistic, and shippable. Android Developers+2Android Developers+2

What you should do next

Since you said not to give branching “if this, do this” advice, here is the sequence:

Next build command

Bash

Next product milestone

Get the Android app to the point where it is ready for Google Play closed testing.

Next technical milestone

After the app is in Play testing, wire the invite flow so your invite link does this:

  • installed users open the app

  • non-installed users go to the Play Store listing

That means your final invite system should be based on:

  • a real published Play listing

  • verified Android App Links

  • no more “mystery browser handoff magic” experiments

Android’s official docs are clear that verified App Links are the proper way to have website URLs open in your app, and Google’s Play docs are clear that Play links are the standard way to send users to install. Android Developers+2Android Developers+2

The plain-English version

Right now you are in the build and stabilize stage.

Your endgame is:

Preview build now
→ Closed testing on Play
→ Published Play listing
→ Invite links that open app if installed, Play Store if not

That is the road to “people can use it” without fighting Android itself.

ChatGPT said:

It should be very doable, not a ground-up rebuild. Since PartyPlus is already built with Expo + React Native, the same codebase can be used to produce iOS builds too, and EAS Build is designed to create ready-to-submit binaries for both Google Play and the Apple App Store. Expo Documentation+1

The honest version

For most of your app, iPhone compatibility is probably a medium job, not a monster job. The core screens, Supabase sync, RSVP flow, and item-claiming logic should mostly carry over because those are cross-platform React Native features. The parts that usually need extra attention are the native/platform edges: app icons and splash, Apple account setup, iOS build config, invite-link behavior on iPhone, and App Store submission/testing through TestFlight. EAS is built specifically to help with that process. Expo Documentation+2Expo Documentation+2

What will actually be required

You will need an Apple Developer account to distribute on iPhone, and the normal iOS path is: create an iOS build, test it with TestFlight, then submit to the App Store through App Store Connect. Apple’s own App Store Connect/TestFlight docs describe that workflow, and Expo’s iOS production guide matches it. Apple Developer+2Expo Documentation+2

The likely technical work list for PartyPlus

Here’s the practical bucket list:

  • add/set the iOS app config in your Expo project

  • create an iOS EAS build

  • test PartyPlus on real iPhones

  • fix any iOS-only UI quirks

  • later, set up the iPhone version of your invite links so installed users open the app cleanly

Because you’re already using EAS on Android, the build side is familiar terrain. The bigger unknown is not “can it run on iPhone?” but “how much cleanup will iPhone testing reveal?” Expo Documentation+2Expo Documentation+2

Your invite-flow concern

You’re absolutely right that an app like this needs both Android and iPhone support to be useful. On iPhone, the polished end-state is the same basic idea as Android: if PartyPlus is installed, the invite link should open the app; if not, the user should go to the App Store listing. On Apple platforms, that typically means using the App Store for install distribution and later using iOS-friendly link handling such as universal-link style behavior. Apple’s distribution model is App Store/TestFlight-centered, not “tap a random web page and silently add the app.” Apple Developer+2Apple Developer+2

My estimate for you

Given where you are now, I’d frame it like this:

  • Getting PartyPlus to build on iPhone: likely very achievable

  • Getting it stable on iPhone: some focused testing work

  • Getting the invite experience polished on iPhone: probably the trickiest piece, but still normal app work, not black magic

So this is not “rewrite the app for Apple.” It is more like add the second runway. The plane is already built. ✈️ Expo Documentation+1

Best next mindset

Do not switch to iPhone work right this second while your Android build is still cooking and your Android release path is still forming. The smart move is:

  1. finish stabilizing the current Android version

  2. get into Google Play closed testing

  3. then do a focused iOS pass using the same Expo/EAS workflow

That keeps you from opening two fronts in the war at once. Apple’s TestFlight path is there when you’re ready, and Expo supports that path directly. Apple Developer+2Expo Documentation+2

Straight answer

How hard will it be?
Not trivial, but nowhere near starting over. For an Expo + React Native app like PartyPlus, it is a real next phase, not a separate project. Expo Documentation+1

When this Android build finishes, the next useful thing is to map the exact road from PartyPlus today to Android closed test first, then iPhone/TestFlight second.

Easiest way to redeploy Netlify

If your invite-web folder already contains the live site files, the fastest path is usually drag-and-drop deploy in Netlify’s web UI.

Do this:

  1. Open Netlify and sign in.

  2. Open your PartyPlus invite site.

  3. Go to the Deploys page for that site.

  4. Find the manual deploy / drag-and-drop area.

  5. Drag the invite-web folder onto it.

Netlify supports manual drag-and-drop deploys of a site folder, and for sites not using Git-based auto-deploys you can also deploy manually from the dashboard. Netlify Docs+2Netlify Docs+2

Which folder to drag

Drag the folder that contains the actual site files, meaning the one with things like:

  • index.html

  • _redirects

  • netlify.toml if present

From what Cody was checking, that sounds like:

invite-web

After you redeploy

Do this exact test:

  1. Open a fresh invite link on your phone

  2. Long-press Open in PartyPlus

  3. Copy the link

  4. Make sure it does not contain:

    • package=com.anonymous.PartyPlusNative

    • intent://

    • #Intent

  5. Tap Open in PartyPlus

What you want is a clean link like:

partyplusnative://party/<id>

If drag-and-drop is not available

That usually means the site is linked to Git or set up differently. Netlify’s docs say manual drag-and-drop deploys are available for manual/local-file workflows, while Git-linked sites normally redeploy from a push to the production branch. Netlify Docs+2Netlify Docs+2

In that case, tell me what you see on the Netlify site page and I’ll tell you the exact next click.
